findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime order_by used here — every optimized request 500s
findings.body: The endpoint passes order_by="-datetime" to OptimizedCursorPaginator, but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value))` / `math.ceil(value)` on the raw attribute value. For a datetime attribute (AuditLogEntry.datetime) this raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime` — which is exactly why DateTimePaginator exists (it converts via strftime first). The exception is raised inside build_cursor when computing the next cursor key, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row will fail with a 500. This path is completely untested and non-functional.

findings.title: Negative-offset slicing is not 'handled automatically' by the Django ORM — it raises AssertionError
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result explicitly enables client-supplied negative cursor offsets (`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` when `enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0`), and the comments claim 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. That is false: Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, producing a 500. The offset is attacker-controllable because cursor strings are parsed from the request query string via Cursor.from_string (`int(bits[1])` accepts negatives), so any superuser/org-admin who enables `optimized_pagination` can crash the endpoint with a crafted cursor. The feature as documented cannot work; the negative-offset branch and its misleading comments should be removed.

findings.title: organization_context.member may be None — AttributeError for token-authenticated requests
findings.body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated whenever the request is not from a superuser and `optimized_pagination=true` is passed. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is None for requests authenticated via org auth tokens/API keys (no member object), so this raises AttributeError and returns a 500 instead of falling back to the normal paginator. Elsewhere in the codebase this is guarded as `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`; the same guard is needed here.

findings.title: Redirect resolution depth cut from 10000 to 1000 silently splits deep segments
findings.body: The redirect-chasing loop now gives up after 1000 hops (previously 10000, with a comment documenting the tradeoff, which was also deleted). When the loop exhausts its iterations, set_span_id remains an intermediate node whose set has already been merged deeper, so the incoming span and its subtree are written to a new, separate set_key and the segment is permanently split — spans that belong to one trace get flushed as two segments with different segment_ids. This failure is silent (no metric, no log). If the lower bound is intentional, the truncation case should at least be detected and emitted as a metric.

findings.title: Eviction threshold hardcoded to 1000 while the configurable max_segment_spans enforcement was removed
findings.body: The Lua script evicts spans whenever a set exceeds a hardcoded 1000 entries (`if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin ... end`), but the threshold is not passed in from Python. At the same time, the Python-side enforcement of the configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) was deleted from SpansBuffer._load_segment_data in buffer.py, so the `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now dead: operators who tune it get no effect, and the effective limit is always 1000 regardless of configuration. Additionally, eviction drops the lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) spans with no metric or log, so data loss from over-large segments is now invisible (previously over-limit segments were skipped with an error log and the `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric).

findings.title: zunionstore default SUM aggregate inflates scores when the same span exists in both sets
findings.body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` uses the default aggregate SUM. With at-least-once Kafka delivery, the same span payload can be present in both the parent set and the span's own set (e.g., after a consumer retry where the redirect map changed between attempts); previously `sunionstore` was idempotent for duplicate members, but now the duplicated member's score is doubled (2 * end_timestamp_precise). Since scores drive the eviction order (zpopmin evicts lowest scores first), duplicated spans are artificially protected from eviction while genuinely earlier spans are evicted instead. Pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to keep merge idempotent.

findings.title: No tests for the new eviction behavior or the reduced redirect depth
findings.body: The PR introduces two data-affecting behaviors in add-buffer.lua — eviction of spans once a segment exceeds 1000 entries (zpopmin) and the redirect-depth reduction from 10000 to 1000 — but the test changes only add the now-required `end_timestamp_precise` field to existing fixtures. There is no test asserting which spans survive eviction (score ordering), that eviction actually caps segment size, or what happens when a redirect chain exceeds the loop limit, so a regression in either behavior (e.g., evicting the root span, off-by-one in the cap) would ship undetected.
